Chapter I

By the time Mara reached the ferry, the river had swallowed the lowest step. Rowan stood beside the ticket window with a lantern in his hand, although it was not yet dark. He had turned the glass toward the wall. This made the room brighter without showing anyone on the opposite bank that it was occupied. Mara had expected to find him packing. Instead, he was carefully drying a child's woollen glove, turning it over whenever the steam began to rise.

"You said you would wait until the bell," Mara told him. "The bell rang an hour ago." Rowan looked at the clock above the window. "I said I would not leave before it rang. That isn't quite the same promise." She might have smiled on any other evening. Now she put the unopened letter beside his cup. The envelope was dry, but her sleeve had left a dark mark on the table. Rowan asked whether her brother had written it. "No. It was written to him. That's why I haven't opened it."

Across the river, the lamps of the old house appeared one by one. Mara counted six and then stopped. Her brother used to light the seventh only when a visitor was expected; after his death, the servants had continued the practice, though no one could have told her for whose sake. When she said that the house looked almost welcoming, Rowan answered that distance was kind to houses. He did not add that it could be kind to people too, but she heard the unspoken words and was grateful that he had left them unspoken.

Chapter II

The next gust lifted the letter from the table. Rowan caught it before it fell into the wet glove, and for a moment Mara saw the address in his lantern light. The handwriting was hers. Not the hurried hand with which she now wrote accounts and instructions, but the round, painstaking letters she had formed as a child. She had addressed the envelope twelve years earlier and hidden it in a book, intending to give it to her brother when she was no longer angry. Until that moment, she had believed she had burned it.

"Then you already know what it says," Rowan said. "I know what I meant," Mara replied. "I'm less certain what I wrote." He handed the envelope back without looking at the seal. She could have thanked him for that, but a spoken thanks would have made a kindness into an agreement, and she did not want him to think she had asked for silence. Instead, she helped him fold the glove. It was too small for either of them. He explained that a passenger had left it that morning, and might come back for it tomorrow.

By then the seventh lamp was burning. Mara did not take it for a summons. She knew how easily a habit could look like a message when one was waiting to receive one. Nevertheless, she asked Rowan whether the boat could still cross. "It can cross," he said. "I haven't said it can come back tonight." She considered this, put the letter inside her coat, and took the lantern from him. Only after they had stepped outside did she turn its glass away from the wall.
